crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Credit Scoring with Alternative Data
children.blurb: Credit scoring with alternative data extends traditional credit assessment beyond bureau files and application data to sources such as rental payments, utility bills, telecom records, bank transaction flows, e-commerce activity, and small business accounting or point-of-sale data.

children.name: Covenant Extraction
children.blurb: Covenant extraction is the use of natural language processing and machine learning to identify, classify, and structure the contractual terms in bond indentures and loan agreements.

children.name: Predicting Distress and Default
children.blurb: Predicting distress and default covers models that estimate the probability a corporate or sovereign borrower will miss payments, enter bankruptcy, or restructure, using financial statements, market prices, news, and alternative data.

children.name: Modelling the Yield Curve
children.blurb: Yield curve modelling in fixed income and credit risk concerns the term structure of interest rates across maturities, from overnight to long dated government and credit instruments.

children.name: Stress Testing Structured Credit
children.blurb: Stress testing structured credit means assessing how tranches of securitized products such as CLOs, ABS, RMBS, and CMBS would perform under severe economic and market shocks, including defaults, prepayments, spread widening, and rating migration.

sections.body: Fixed income and credit risk is the part of finance concerned with lending, bond prices, and the chance a borrower fails to pay. Artificial intelligence is now used to read loan applications and alternative data for credit scoring, to pull rules out of bond and loan contracts, to flag companies that may default, to fit yield curve shapes, and to run stress tests on bundles of loans. These are working systems, not research demos, used by banks, insurers and asset managers. The work is narrow and specific: a model may estimate a probability of default or extract a covenant from a document, but it does not make lending decisions on its own.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some tasks are fairly mature. Credit scoring with alternative data and yield curve fitting are widely deployed, and covenant extraction has become reliable enough for routine contract review. Distress prediction and structured credit stress testing are less settled, because defaults are rare and past crises do not repeat cleanly. The honest limits are data quality, regime change and explainability. A model trained on calm markets can miss a sudden liquidity shock, and a credit score built from phone or transaction data may be biased in ways that are hard to audit. No system here can promise certainty about a borrower or a bond.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader wanting to see how lenders use non-traditional signals should start with Credit Scoring with Alternative Data, which covers the data sources and the fairness problems. Covenant Extraction explains how language models pull obligations and restrictions from legal text, and why human review still matters. Predicting Distress and Default connects accounting, market and news signals to early warning scores, while Modelling the Yield Curve shows how neural networks and other methods fit and forecast interest rates across maturities. Stress Testing Structured Credit ties these together by showing how shocks to rates, defaults and covenants flow through securitized products. Together the pages move from a single borrower to a whole portfolio.
